item.title: Sha EK Sentenced To Five Years For Bronx Shooting
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Sha EK receives a five-year sentence as the Bronx case over gunfire that injured three people reaches a new court outcome.
item.content:encoded:
Sha EK received a five-year prison sentence on November 17 in the Bronx shooting case that left three people injured.

The 23-year-old rapper’s sentencing follows a September 21 guilty plea to second-degree conspiracy, according to the Bronx District Attorney’s court calendar. News 12 reported the prison term after Tuesday’s proceeding.

The case centers on gunfire at the Patterson Houses in Mott Haven. Prosecutors said the attack targeted a rival gang member in retaliation for another gang member’s death the previous day.

Two bystanders were injured along with the intended target. The district attorney’s calendar identifies July 22, 2024, as the shooting date and places it on East 145th Street.

Authorities arrested Sha EK months after the shooting. AllHipHop reported the original charges in February 2025, when the case included attempted murder, assault and weapons allegations.

The sentence arrives four years after Sha EK’s major-label breakthrough. He signed with Warner Records in 2022 and released Face Of The What, turning attention from his drill records to his broader career.

In an interview with AllHipHop, Sha EK described recording during lockdown before finding his footing in drill. He said his friends encouraged him and explained how posting his own music helped him build an audience.

The rapper pointed to “D&D” and its spread on TikTok as an important step toward label interest. Before signing, he had distributed his work through UnitedMasters and posted on Instagram, Apple Music and YouTube.

“I was getting paid independently, but now that I am signed, the money different,” Sha EK told AllHipHop.

He also spoke about how the deal changed his family’s circumstances. He had moved to New Jersey and said he could help his mother, sister, brother and the people around him.

Sha EK later met with roughly 20 students from Usher’s New Look program at the Universal Hip Hop Museum. During that visit, he discussed his experiences as a young recording artist and his approach to lyrics. He said he wanted his music to reach more listeners, including his daughter, and avoided naming people in songs.

The district attorney’s calendar listed his sentencing before Judge Mitchell in Part 11.

item.title: Howard University, Cardi B And The Future Of The Music Business
item.dc:creator: Chuck Creekmur (@ChuckCreekmur)
item.description: Chuck "Jigsaw" Creekmur guest lectured at Howard University. Here's what he experienced.
item.content:encoded:
A week ago, earlier this month of November 2026, I had the unique privilege of speaking at Howard University, where I delivered a lecture rooted in the remarkable rise of Cardi B.

Now, before anybody gets their panties in a bunch, this wasn’t about celebrity gossip, rap beef or even the music itself. This was about the BUSINESS of Cardi B.

Media. Marketing. Branding. Strategy. Ownership. The machinery behind the superstar.

I had the pleasure of engaging with students at Howard University in an interactive session organized by the incredible Jazz Young, whom I’ve known for many years. I knew Jazz during her days in the music industry, and watching her evolve into this educational powerhouse has been a beautiful thing. She’s now helping prepare the next generation of executives, entrepreneurs and creative minds.

What’s especially interesting is that this whole thing started with a conversation Jazz and I had about a year ago. We discussed the possibility of building an entire course around a single artist, examining not simply their music, but the business ecosystem that makes their success possible.

We tossed around several names before landing on Cardi B. We wanted somebody culturally relevant, commercially successful and, most importantly, somebody the students could genuinely connect with.

Cardi was a perfect case study.

I had interviewed Cardi back in 2016, when she was still on Love & Hip Hop and her future as a global superstar was far from guaranteed. Even then, I saw someone with tremendous ambition, personality and a remarkable understanding of who she was. This was 10 years ago to the month. 

Fast forward to today, and Cardi B represents something much bigger than hit records. She represents the evolution of raw ambition into a sophisticated business enterprise.

And that’s what we explored.

We talked about publicity, brand partnerships, marketing campaigns, stage production, street teams, media strategy and the countless professionals whose work often happens outside the spotlight. Pat Parks, another lead professor in the program, helped refine the lecture and also guide the flow of the class. 

Here’s something I’ve learned after nearly three decades in this industry: Talent may get you through the door, but understanding the business can determine how long you stay in the building.

What made this experience particularly rewarding was the students themselves.

These young people were SHARP.

They were informed, curious, articulate and ready to engage. This wasn’t one of those situations where an old industry guy stands in front of a classroom telling everybody how things used to be. We had a real exchange of ideas.

At one point, we turned the tables.

Instead of me answering all the questions, I became the interviewer. Students stepped in front of the camera and presented their ideas, discussed brand partnerships and explained the business decisions behind Cardi’s expanding empire.

And they delivered.

You could see their preparation, their confidence and their ability to think critically about the intersection of culture and commerce. Some of them already carried themselves like professionals ready to enter the industry tomorrow.

That was probably my favorite part of the entire experience.

We live in an era where everybody wants to be the star. Everybody wants the followers, the likes, the viral moment and the applause. And there’s nothing inherently wrong with any of that. And yet, it has gotten problematic. 

But somebody has to negotiate the deals. Somebody has to build the marketing strategy. Somebody has to understand the contracts, manage the relationships, produce the shows and create opportunities that extend beyond the next hit song. That’s how it was in the “mogul era,” which coincided with Hip-Hop’s Golden 90s.

Those people are just as essential to the culture as the artists themselves.

And sitting in that classroom at Howard, I was reminded that the future of our industry isn’t exclusively on a stage, inside a recording booth or in front of a camera.

Some of that future was sitting right in front of me.

There’s another part of this experience that really stayed with me: the importance of professionals reaching back.

Those of us who have spent decades building businesses, navigating the industry and learning lessons the hard way have a responsibility to share that knowledge. Not simply to tell stories about our accomplishments, but to give younger people information they can actually use.

And we should be willing to learn from them, too.

The industry they’re entering is not the same one I entered. Technology has changed. Media has changed. The relationship between artists and audiences has changed. The business models are constantly evolving.

That exchange between experience and fresh perspective is where real progress happens.

I’m grateful to Jazz Young, Professor Pat, Howard University and every student who participated in this experience. They reminded me why education, mentorship and access remain so important.

The next generation of Hip-Hop executives, innovators and cultural architects is already preparing for its moment.

And based on what I witnessed at Howard University, the future is Bison bright.

We’ve just got to make sure we’re doing our part to help them get there.

And do remember, this was a serious academic examination of Hip-Hop as culture, commerce and a career.

item.title: Marvin Sapp Defends Roc Nation Deal, Says He’s Keeping It “Churchy” & “Funky”
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Marvin Sapp defends his Roc Nation distribution deal and names the gospel stars he would bring to a Super Bowl halftime show.
item.content:encoded:
Marvin Sapp is defending his Roc Nation partnership while arguing for gospel music to headline the Super Bowl.

In a new Associated Press interview, the singer said his distribution arrangement lets him own the master for Restoration. The album arrives Friday, November 20.

Working with a company rooted in Hip-Hop has drawn questions from gospel listeners, but Sapp said his musical priorities remain intact.

“I’m keeping it Christ-centered, churchy and funky all at the same time,” he told AP.

He also named Kirk Franklin as his choice to assemble a gospel halftime lineup. His proposed participants included the Clark Sisters, Kim Burrell, Deitrick Haddon and Fred Hammond, with Sapp himself eager to join.

That vision comes as Sapp continues dealing with the fallout from a viral church offering clip. He told AP that the backlash brought death threats and police protection.

The clip showed him requesting donations toward a $40,000 offering goal. Organizers said doors were not locked and nobody was held against their will, describing the instruction to close them as a security measure.

The distribution agreement was announced in July, rather than this week. In an interview with Christianity Today, Sapp described the business distinction that informed his decision.

“A distributor takes the finished product and takes it to places and spaces where it might not otherwise be heard,” he said.

Sapp told the publication that he keeps his masters and gives Roc Nation a smaller share of earnings than under his former label arrangement. Producer Stanley Brown, who leads Timeless Music Group, brokered the partnership.

The criticism has focused partly on Jay-Z’s public image and whether that association fits a gospel artist. Christianity Today also reported that Hezekiah Walker reached his own distribution agreement with Roc Nation in September.

Sapp’s music has already reached prominent listeners outside the gospel circuit. In 2020, Justin Bieber performed his “Never Would Have Made It” with Kanye West’s Sunday Service Choir, an appearance Kim Kardashian documented online.

That gathering also featured music by Roddy Ricch and Nas. Bieber had previously expressed interest in joining one of West’s weekly gospel events before making the appearance.

For now, Sapp is preparing to release his 17th album.

item.title: DMX’s Private Prayers Reach Readers In Estate-Curated Book With Rakim
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: DMX's estate brings his handwritten spiritual reflections into print, with Rakim contributing to the new collection.
item.content:encoded:
DMX‘s prayers are finding a life beyond the stage, as his estate opens a personal archive for a new book that just arrived.

The Gospel According to DMX brings Rakim into the project as a foreword contributor. The collection draws from material DMX left behind, including spiritual reflections he scribbled on hotel stationery, receipts and napkins.

His daughter Sasha Simmons and fiancee Desiree Lindstrom, the estate’s co-administrators, curated the volume, according to publisher Simon & Schuster. Alongside prayers and sermons, it reproduces handwritten pages that have not been made public before.

The hardcover edition has a faux-leather cover, gold-like page edges and a ribbon bookmark. Selected lyrics appear alongside the prayers and sermons, and the estate has retained DMX’s archival writings in their original form.

The publisher’s announcement also names his spiritual adviser, Pastor Apostle Barbara King, among the foreword writers. An appendix gathers passages from the Book of Psalms, adding another part of the religious material that informed his writing.

Faith was already part of the story DMX told about himself. In an interview for TV One’s Uncensored, he considered how he would account for his life, including its difficult stretches.

“I’m gonna look back on my life just before I go and thank God for every moment,” DMX said.

AllHipHop previously reported on the posthumous airing of that interview, which gave viewers his own reflections after his death. DMX died April 9, 2021, at 50.

The Yonkers rapper had already put his story on the page during his lifetime. His autobiography arrived in 2003, and BET later followed him for the reality series DMX: Soul of a Man in 2006.

The book also adds to a legacy built through Ruff Ryders, where DMX’s rise helped propel a movement alongside Eve and The LOX. His first five albums debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, starting with It’s Dark and Hell Is Hot in 1998.

That same year, Flesh of My Flesh, Blood of My Blood became his second chart-topping album. Years later, his posthumous album Exodus was named after his youngest son.

The Gospel According to DMX runs 208 pages.

item.title: D-Nice Residency Anchors Thanksgiving Week Of Atlanta Food Giveaways
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: D-Nice's Georgia residency gets a community lead-in as Atlanta and Clayton County prepare Thanksgiving food distributions.
item.content:encoded:
D-Nice‘s Thanksgiving residency in metro Atlanta will follow two community food events aimed at helping families get through the holiday.

The Arena at Southlake announced its “Feast Week” program. Before the music starts in Morrow, the venue and operator TRP Now will join organizations distributing groceries and other essentials.

“Thanksgiving is about gratitude first, so Feast Week feeds families before a single ticket is scanned,” TRP Now executive Rashid Mausi told AllHipHop. Mausi described the concerts as a chance for Clayton County to celebrate locally.

The first stop is Liberty Plaza in Atlanta on November 23 at 11:30 A.M. Organizers expect to serve more than 750 people through “We Feed The Block,” with food boxes, supplies and access to community resources.

Jazze Pha helped establish that initiative alongside Jevon Dewand, Sebastiana Laremont and attorney Gerald Griggs. The producer and Dewand are also scheduled to perform at the gathering.

On November 24, the arena will host Area in Need and Missionary House for their 10th annual Thanksgiving grocery giveaway. Families can visit between 11 A.M. and 2:30 P.M. at 1300 Southlake Circle, Suite 2000, in Morrow.

The venue’s concert listing puts D-Nice’s two-night run on November 27 and 28. Too $hort, David Banner, Machel Montano and Digable Planets are among the performers listed for Friday, with Queen Latifah on Saturday’s bill.

That mix reaches across generations of rap while making room for R&B and soca. The arena describes the shows as a residency built around D-Nice, whose recording and DJ career stretches from Boogie Down Productions to his pandemic-era Club Quarantine sets.

His party platform has supported charitable work before. In 2020, D-Nice partnered with Will Smith’s Bel-Air Athletics on a Club Quarantine hoodie benefiting coronavirus relief, with half of each hoodie’s net proceeds earmarked for the CDC Foundation’s response fund.

This time, the organizers have separated the food distributions from the Thanksgiving-weekend performances. The community events take place before the ticketed shows, not inside them.

Doors for both concert nights open at 7 p.m., with performances scheduled to begin at 8 P.M.

item.title: Freddie Jackson Gets El DeBarge Tribute As Soul Train Awards Return To Chicago
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Freddie Jackson's Soul Train salute pairs his legacy with El DeBarge as BET brings the ceremony to CBS for the first time.
item.content:encoded:
Freddie Jackson will be remembered by another voice from R&B’s 1980s run when El DeBarge honors him on the Soul Train Awards telecast. BET announced the tribute Tuesday, adding a memorial for the Harlem singer to its Chicago celebration.

The performance follows Jackson’s October 5 death, which his family confirmed in a public statement. His recording career stretched across decades, with the ballads “You Are My Lady” and “Rock Me Tonight (For Old Times Sake)” among his early breakthroughs.

DeBarge’s tribute is part of a lineup that also pairs Muni Long with Lucky Daye for a medley, according to BET’s announcement. Kirk Franklin is on the bill, while Common and Chance the Rapper are among the presenters.

“The Soul Train Awards has always celebrated the music that moves us, wherever it comes from,” said Connie Orlando, EVP, Specials, Music Programming & Music Strategy, BET. “Honoring Freddie and Dolly while spotlighting the artists shaping R&B and soul right now is exactly what this stage was built for.”

Jackson’s route to the charts started in church. At Harlem’s White Rock Baptist Church, he met Paul Laurence, the songwriter and producer who later helped build his solo career. Before Capitol released his debut, Jackson worked with Mystic Merlin and sang behind Melba Moore.

That 1985 debut, Rock Me Tonight, delivered two consecutive No. 1 R&B singles. The title track spent six weeks at the top, and “You Are My Lady” also crossed into the pop Top 20, reaching No. 13.

He followed it with Just Like the First Time in 1986. Both albums reached platinum status, and songs including “Jam Tonight” and “Have You Ever Loved Somebody” extended his run on R&B radio. He continued recording well beyond that initial success, releasing For You in 2010 and Love Signals in 2018 before adding My First Love to his catalog in 2023.

The awards will also recognize Chaka Khan, Durand Bernarr and Elmiene, with each artist performing. Another tribute brings Mickey Guyton, Brittney Spencer and steel guitarist Robert Randolph together to honor Dolly Parton.

Chicago connects the show to the city where Soul Train began. This year’s broadcast also expands its television reach, with CBS carrying the ceremony alongside BET for the first time.

The Soul Train Awards air on November 27 at 8 P.M. ET/PT.

item.title: Jay-Z Brings His ‘Fade To Black’ Farewell Film To YouTube
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Jay-Z opens his documentary vault as 'Fade To Black' gets a scheduled YouTube premiere revisiting his famous farewell.
item.content:encoded:
Jay-Z is bringing his old farewell to YouTube with a November 18 premiere of the 2004 documentary “Fade To Black.”

His official artist channel has scheduled the film for noon ET, matching an announcement sent through his JAŸ-Z30 mailing list. The premiere page is already live, but the documentary has not started streaming.

“Fade To Black” follows the Madison Square Garden concert Jay-Z staged in November 2003 while presenting “The Black Album” as his farewell to solo recording.

The film’s production company, RadicalMedia, describes a documentary that moves between the album’s creation and the Garden performance. That means the story extends beyond a concert set list to the work that went into the record.

Beyoncé, Mary J. Blige, Missy Elliott, Foxy Brown and Pharrell are among the performers named in the company’s synopsis. Rick Rubin, Dame Dash and Slick Rick also appear, putting collaborators and fellow artists inside the portrait of that period.

When AllHipHop reported the film’s original release, Jay-Z framed the Garden show as the realization of an ambition that started long before the arena bookings. His statement connected the occasion directly to his Brooklyn beginnings.

“This was the ultimate dream growing up in Brooklyn. I went from Marcy to Madison Square,” Jay-Z said at the time.

Pat Paulson and Michael John Warren directed the documentary, which Jay-Z narrated. Paramount Classics handled its theatrical release, while Jay-Z also served as an executive producer through Marcy Projects Productions. Paramount’s current catalog credits Bob Ezrin, Rich Kleiman and Justin Wilkes as the film’s producers.

The new premiere gives that period another place on his own channel during the JAŸ-Z30 campaign. His official website currently uses the anniversary branding “’96 & Forever,” alongside links to watch and listen to “JAŸ-Z In ∞.”

For viewers following the new announcement, the distinction matters: Wednesday’s scheduled presentation concerns an existing film about the 2003 concert and recording sessions. The email does not announce a sequel, additional footage or a newly filmed performance.

“Fade To Black” originally reached theaters on November 5, 2004.

item.title: Nick Cannon Blames His Ego For Mariah Carey Split
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Nick Cannon faces frank feedback from his oldest children as his family prepares to step into Netflix's reality spotlight.
item.content:encoded:
Nick Cannon puts his own ego at the center of his split from Mariah Carey in the trailer for his family’s Netflix series. Their oldest children aren’t staying out of the conversation, either.

“My ego drove me away from Mariah,” Cannon says in the Raising the Cannons preview, according to Page Six. The trailer introduces a show about the demands of raising his children while keeping his entertainment career moving.

Monroe has her own explanation for why her parents haven’t reunited. “If you didn’t have all these kids, you would have been back together,” she tells her father, Page Six reports.

Her twin brother, Moroccan, also questions whether Cannon can keep living this way. Those comments come from the preview, not a newly announced change in Cannon and Carey’s relationship.

The twins are 15, and Cannon describes them as advisers rather than children who simply follow his lead. In Netflix’s introduction to the family, he says their opinions carry weight when he considers his relationships.

“They’re the parents, I’m the kid,” Cannon tells Tudum. He also describes his current co-parenting arrangement with Carey in positive terms, saying the two remain in regular contact about parenting and future plans. Cannon and Carey divorced in 2016, when the twins were 5 years old.

That gives the series more to work with than a rundown of who lives where. Cannon’s account of how he and Carey function now sits alongside the teenagers’ questions about decisions he made after their marriage.

Cannon has 12 children with six women: Carey, Brittany Bell, Abby De La Rosa, Alyssa Scott, Bre Tiesi and LaNisha Cole. Netflix says the series follows his family responsibilities, work and health challenges.

He has already acknowledged that coordinating those households isn’t simple. In an interview with Maury Povich, Cannon said a group chat involving the six mothers went badly after he tried bringing everyone into one conversation.

Cannon hadn’t revealed the show’s name during that conversation, although he said it was coming in December. The newly released preview now gives that project a title and a firm place on Netflix’s calendar.

Raising the Cannons premieres December 18.

item.title: Kevin Gates’ $94K Support Order Faces Recalculation After Income Review
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Kevin Gates' divorce payments face a new calculation after the court revisits the earnings behind his support obligations.
item.content:encoded:
Kevin Gates could see his monthly support payments change after a judge ordered a new calculation based on lower income figures.

Court documents filed Monday describe the review of his financial obligations to estranged wife Dreka Gates, according to TMZ. The court had set support at $94,223 a month in June, dividing that amount between spousal and child support.

The income calculation is now central to the dispute. The earlier hearing used alleged monthly earnings of $184,707, which included royalties that affected the picture of Gates’ income.

For April through June, the court is now using about $54,496 a month. July through November carries a different figure, roughly $75,000 monthly, TMZ reported.

Those revisions will affect calculations for payments covering both periods. Dreka’s attorneys have been directed to work out new support amounts using the updated numbers.

The June order assigned $56,997 monthly to spousal support and $37,226 to child support. A revised payment total remains to be calculated.

Money from Gates’ music had already become a major part of the divorce proceedings. AllHipHop previously covered his response to a catalog proceeds order benefiting Dreka.

Asked about that catalog order in an interview on “The TMZ Podcast,” Gates described his willingness to give to loved ones. “I ain’t mad at nothing. I’m blessed,” he said when asked whether sharing the proceeds angered him.

His comments about parenting took a more personal turn. Gates recalled his children enjoying cardboard forts and explained how spending time together had changed his understanding of providing for them.

The divorce filing dates to July 30, 2025, in Los Angeles. Dreka cited irreconcilable differences and sought joint legal and physical custody of their two children, Islah and Khaza.

Her petition also requested spousal support and coverage of her legal fees. She listed July 10, 2025, as the separation date after a wedding in October 2015.

Gates has also disputed the legal status of their marriage. He said their Islamic ceremony was not followed by the paperwork needed for legal recognition, despite their years of presenting themselves as a married couple.

Dreka’s earlier monthly support request totaled $73,467, comprising $46,274 in spousal support and $27,193 for the children.

item.title: Smoke Says He’s Retired As Field Mob Partners Grow Apart
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Smoke opens up about life after Field Mob, explaining why he and Shawn Jay have gone their separate ways over time.
item.content:encoded:
Smoke says he’s retired from rap, and his relationship with Field Mob partner Shawn Jay has changed as his priorities have shifted.

The Georgia artist discussed the duo’s distance during a November 15 interview on The Big Facts Network. He described himself as a content creator while looking back at their partnership. “But I’m retired,” Smoke said.

“But now like we just grown. We grew apart from each other. We grew away from each other,” Smoke said.

His account follows years of solo work alongside the Field Mob name. Smoke previously described branching out as something he wanted without abandoning the group.

His solo plans were not presented as a breakup when he spoke with AllHipHop in 2013. Smoke treated recording on his own as another business opportunity, describing age and changing interests as reasons to try something different.

Field Mob had previously taken that partnership to Ludacris’ Disturbing Tha Peace label. When the deal was announced, Ludacris told AllHipHop he wanted a wider audience to recognize the pair’s Southern lyricism.

In a 2013 interview with AllHipHop, he explained how putting the duo first had delayed his individual ambitions.

“I been wanting to do it, I just never did it because I always put Field Mob first,” Smoke said then.

That conversation came as he prepared his debut solo mixtape, K.A.N.G. He said listeners’ interest in his individual recordings encouraged him to pursue the project.

Smoke and Shawn Jay built Field Mob in Albany, Georgia, before releasing their debut album, 613: Ashy to Classy, in 2000. Their catalog includes “Sick of Being Lonely” and the Ciara collaboration “So What.”

Their second album, From Da Roota To Tha Toota, included “Sick of Being Lonely.” Jazze Pha later produced “So What,” pairing the two rappers with Ciara for another recognizable part of their catalog.

The duo also used their hometown to explain the Light Poles and Pine Trees title, contrasting Albany’s surroundings with better-known city landmarks.

“There’s no arch like in St. Louis or palm trees like California,” Smoke told AllHipHop. “You look up and that’s what you see in Albany.”

Field Mob’s third album, Light Poles and Pine Trees, arrived in 2006.
